items.q: Which statement best describes the reactions in the flask at 20 s?
options: The forward rate is greater than the reverse rate.
The forward and reverse rates are equal, so [NO<sub>2</sub>] is constant.
The forward reaction runs by itself until the N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> is used up.
The reverse rate is greater than the forward rate, so N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> is being re-formed.

items.q: Use the graph to calculate [N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>] once the system has reached equilibrium.

mistakes.why: Value: you subtracted the NO₂ formed straight from the N₂O₄. Each N₂O₄ that reacts gives two NO₂, so N₂O₄ falls by half of 0.0400 M.
Value: 0.0200 M is how much N₂O₄ reacted, not how much is left. Subtract it from the starting 0.0500 M.

items.q: From 50 s on, [NO<sub>2</sub>] stays at 0.0400 M. Which statement explains why?
options: NO<sub>2</sub> forms and reacts away at equal rates.
The N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> has run out, so no more NO<sub>2</sub> can form.
The molecules have stopped colliding because the flask has cooled.
The concentrations of N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> and NO<sub>2</sub> have become equal.

items.q: In a second trial at the same temperature, the student fills the same flask with 0.100 M NO<sub>2</sub> and no N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>. What is [NO<sub>2</sub>] once the system reaches equilibrium?
Which feature of the graph shows that the system has reached equilibrium?
options: The curve becomes flat.
The curve passes through half of its final value.
The curve is at its steepest, at the very start of the experiment.
[NO<sub>2</sub>] reaches the starting value of [N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>].

items.q: Based on the diagrams, which is the earliest time shown at which the system is known to be at equilibrium?
options: t<sub>2</sub>
t<sub>1</sub>
t<sub>3</sub>

items.q: Which statement describes what happens in the container between t<sub>2</sub> and t<sub>3</sub>?
options: XY forms and breaks apart at equal rates.
No molecules react, because the reaction is complete.
XY molecules keep forming, but XY molecules no longer break apart into X<sub>2</sub> and Y<sub>2</sub>.
X<sub>2</sub> and Y<sub>2</sub> keep reacting until one of them runs out.

items.q: Between t = 0 and t<sub>2</sub>, how many XY molecules form for each X<sub>2</sub> molecule that reacts?
A student says, "At equilibrium there should be equal numbers of reactant and product molecules, so the system at t<sub>3</sub> is not at equilibrium." Which response is correct?
options: Wrong claim: equilibrium needs unchanging counts, as at t<sub>2</sub> and t<sub>3</sub>.
Right claim: there are more XY molecules than X<sub>2</sub> molecules, so the forward reaction is still ahead.
Right claim: equilibrium is reached when half of the reactant molecules have turned into product.
Wrong claim: the system is at equilibrium because the X<sub>2</sub> molecules have reacted away.

items.q: A sealed flask holds H<sub>2</sub>, I<sub>2</sub> and HI at equilibrium: H<sub>2</sub>(g) + I<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 HI(g). A tiny amount of I<sub>2</sub> made of a radioactive iodine isotope is swapped in for the same amount of ordinary I<sub>2</sub>, so the concentrations do not change. Later, radioactive iodine atoms are found in HI molecules. What does this show?
options: The forward reaction still runs at equilibrium.
The system was not at equilibrium before the swap.
The radioactive isotope made the forward reaction faster than the reverse reaction.
Reactions at equilibrium have stopped, and the label moved into HI molecules through mixing of the gases.

items.q: Solid calcium carbonate decomposes when heated: CaCO<sub>3</sub>(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO<sub>2</sub>(g). A sample is heated in an open dish. Why does this system not reach equilibrium?
options: CO<sub>2</sub> escapes, so it rarely meets CaO to react back.
Solids are not able to take part in reversible reactions.
The forward reaction is too slow to reach equilibrium at any temperature.
Heating makes the reverse reaction faster than the forward reaction.

items.q: Pure N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> is sealed in a flask at constant temperature. Predict how each quantity changes during the first minute, before equilibrium is reached: N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 NO<sub>2</sub>(g).

variables.name: Total mass of gas in the flask

items.q: H<sub>2</sub> and I<sub>2</sub> are sealed in a flask and react: H<sub>2</sub>(g) + I<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 HI(g). Put the events in the order they happen.
options: Only the forward reaction can occur, because no HI is present yet.
HI builds up, and HI molecules begin to react to re-form H<sub>2</sub> and I<sub>2</sub>.
The forward rate falls and the reverse rate rises as reactants are used up and HI accumulates.
The two rates become equal, and every concentration stays constant from then on.

items.q: A flask starts with 0.0800 M N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> and no NO<sub>2</sub>: N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 NO<sub>2</sub>(g). At equilibrium, [N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>] = 0.0520 M. Calculate [NO<sub>2</sub>] at equilibrium.

mistakes.why: Value: 0.0280 M is how much N₂O₄ reacted. Each N₂O₄ gives two NO₂, so multiply by 2.
Value: you divided by 2. The coefficient 2 is on NO₂, so NO₂ rises twice as much as N₂O₄ falls.

items.q: Which statement is true of every system at chemical equilibrium?
options: The concentrations stay constant over time.
The concentrations of reactants and products are equal.
The forward and reverse reactions have both stopped.
The reaction has gone to completion.

items.q: In the flask from the notes, N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 NO<sub>2</sub>(g), the reverse reaction speeds up as NO<sub>2</sub> forms. Which explanation at the particle level is best?
options: More NO<sub>2</sub> per liter means more NO<sub>2</sub>-NO<sub>2</sub> collisions.
NO<sub>2</sub> molecules move faster as they form, so they collide harder.
The N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> molecules push the NO<sub>2</sub> molecules together.
The forward reaction releases energy that drives the reverse reaction.

items.q: Which observations would tell you that a reaction in a sealed flask has reached equilibrium? Select all that apply.
options: The color of the gas mixture stops changing.
The pressure inside the flask, at constant temperature, stops changing.
The flask contains equal amounts of reactants and products.
Bubbles of gas keep forming at a steady rate in the liquid.

items.q: What do the double half-arrows (⇌) in a chemical equation tell you?
options: The reaction can run in both directions.
The reaction is twice as fast as one written with a single arrow.
The reactants and products are present in equal amounts.
The reaction gives off heat to the surroundings.

items.q: Which statement describes the vessel at 0 s?
options: The net reaction goes in reverse: isobutane is turning into butane overall.
The net reaction goes forward, because the forward reaction is written first.
The system is at equilibrium, because both reactions are happening.
The net reaction goes forward, because more isobutane is present than butane.

items.q: What happens to the concentration of butane between 0 s and 80 s, and why?
options: It rises: the reverse reaction makes butane faster than the forward reaction uses it.
It falls, because the forward reaction uses butane up.
It stays the same, because the total amount of C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub> gas in the vessel is constant.
It rises, because the forward rate increases over the same time.

items.q: Of the times in the table, which is the first at which the system is at equilibrium?
options: 0 s

items.q: Which particle-level explanation accounts for the rise in the forward rate over time?
options: More butane per liter means more butane reacts each second.
Isobutane molecules collide with butane and push it to react.
The molecules speed up as the reaction continues.
The catalyst is used up, so the forward reaction takes over.

items.q: Calculate the net rate at which butane forms at 0 s.

mistakes.why: Value: you added the two rates. Butane forms by the reverse reaction and is used by the forward reaction, so subtract.
Value: the sign is reversed. Butane is being formed overall, so its net rate of formation is positive.

items.q: Right after the H<sub>2</sub> is injected at 100 s, how do the two rates compare?
options: The forward rate is now greater than the reverse rate.
The reverse rate is now greater than the forward rate.
Both rates increase by the same amount, so they stay equal.
Both rates stay the same, because the temperature did not change.

items.q: Which evidence from the graph shows that the net reaction runs forward after 100 s?
options: [HI] rises while [I<sub>2</sub>] falls.
[H<sub>2</sub>] jumps up at 100 s.
[H<sub>2</sub>] ends higher than it was before 100 s.
The three curves are flat before 100 s.

items.q: Use the information given to calculate [HI] at the new equilibrium.

mistakes.why: Value: HI rises by twice as much as I₂ falls, because of the coefficient 2 on HI. Double the change in [I₂].
Value: HI is a product of the net forward reaction, so its concentration goes up, not down.

items.q: Compare the forward rate at 200 s with the forward rate at 50 s.
options: It is higher at 200 s, and the reverse rate is just as high.
It is the same, because both times are at equilibrium.
It is higher at 200 s, and the reverse rate is lower.
It is lower at 200 s, because some H<sub>2</sub> has been used up.

items.q: In a sealed flask, the forward rate of 2 SO<sub>2</sub>(g) + O<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 SO<sub>3</sub>(g) is 5.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> M/s and the reverse rate is 2.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> M/s. Which statement is correct?
options: [SO<sub>3</sub>] is increasing.
[SO<sub>3</sub>] is decreasing.
[SO<sub>3</sub>] is constant.
[O<sub>2</sub>] is increasing.

items.q: For N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 NO<sub>2</sub>(g), the rate of each reaction is given per N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> molecule: N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> splits at 6.0 × 10<sup>−4</sup> M/s and re-forms at 2.5 × 10<sup>−4</sup> M/s. Calculate the net rate at which [NO<sub>2</sub>] increases.

mistakes.why: Value: that is the net rate for N₂O₄. Each N₂O₄ that splits makes two NO₂ (and two NO₂ re-form each N₂O₄), so double it.
Value: you halved the net rate. The coefficient 2 is on NO₂, so NO₂ changes twice as fast as N₂O₄.

items.q: H<sub>2</sub>(g) + I<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 HI(g) is at equilibrium in a sealed flask. Some HI is suddenly removed. Predict each quantity.

variables.name: Forward rate, at the moment HI is removed
Reverse rate, at the moment HI is removed

items.q: A system A(g) ⇌ B(g) is at equilibrium. More A is added. Put the events in order.
options: [A] increases at constant temperature.
The forward rate increases, so it is now greater than the reverse rate.
A net forward reaction uses A and makes B.
The forward rate falls and the reverse rate rises until they are equal again.

items.q: The system 2 NO<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>(g) is at equilibrium. Which changes, made at constant temperature, would make the reverse rate greater than the forward rate for a while? Select all that apply.
options: Adding N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>
Removing some NO<sub>2</sub>
Adding NO<sub>2</sub>
Removing some N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>

items.q: A catalyst is added to a system that is already at equilibrium. What happens?
options: Both rates increase by the same factor, so there is no net reaction.
The forward rate increases more, so more product forms.
The reverse rate increases more, so more reactant forms.
Both rates decrease, because the catalyst takes up reactant particles.

items.q: In a flask at constant temperature, [CO<sub>2</sub>] is falling for CO(g) + H<sub>2</sub>O(g) ⇌ CO<sub>2</sub>(g) + H<sub>2</sub>(g). Which statement must be true at this moment?
options: The reverse rate is greater than the forward rate.
The forward rate is greater than the reverse rate.
The forward reaction has stopped.
[H<sub>2</sub>] is rising.

items.q: For A(g) ⇌ B(g) in a sealed flask, B is removed as fast as it forms. Which statement describes the system?
options: It does not reach equilibrium; the reverse rate stays low.
It reaches equilibrium faster, because B is out of the way of the A molecules.
It reaches equilibrium when [A] equals [B].
It stops reacting once half of the A is gone.

items.q: Calculate the reaction quotient, Q<sub>c</sub>, for flask 1.

mistakes.why: Value: you left out the exponents. Each concentration is raised to the power of its coefficient: [SO₃]² and [SO₂]².
Value: you put the reactants on top. Q is products over reactants, just like K.
Value: you squared [SO₃] but not [SO₂]. Its coefficient is also 2.

items.q: For flask 2, Q<sub>c</sub> = 400. Which way does the net reaction go as flask 2 approaches equilibrium?
options: In reverse, because Q > K: there is too much product for equilibrium.
Forward, because Q > K means the forward reaction is faster.
Forward, because flask 2 holds more SO<sub>3</sub> than SO<sub>2</sub>.
No net reaction, because Q and K are both greater than 1.

items.q: Which flask is already at equilibrium when it is prepared?
options: Flask 3
Flask 1
Flask 2
Flask 4

items.q: What happens in flask 4 after it is prepared?
options: SO<sub>3</sub> forms, because Q = 0 is less than K.
Nothing, because there is no SO<sub>3</sub> to react.
SO<sub>2</sub> forms, because Q is less than K.
Q is undefined, because [SO<sub>3</sub>] is zero.

items.q: A student says flask 1 will react in reverse because it contains the most SO<sub>3</sub>. Which response is best?
options: Disagree: Q = 80.0 is less than K, so flask 1 reacts forward and makes more SO<sub>3</sub>.
Agree: the flask with the most product reacts in reverse.
Disagree: flask 1 is at equilibrium because it has more SO<sub>3</sub> than SO<sub>2</sub>.
Agree: Q = 80.0 is greater than 1, so the net reaction goes in reverse.

items.q: Which expression is K<sub>p</sub> for this reaction?
options: P<sub>NH₃</sub><sup>2</sup> / (P<sub>N₂</sub> × P<sub>H₂</sub><sup>3</sup>)
[NH<sub>3</sub>]<sup>2</sup> / ([N<sub>2</sub>][H<sub>2</sub>]<sup>3</sup>)
2 P<sub>NH₃</sub> / (P<sub>N₂</sub> × 3 P<sub>H₂</sub>)
(P<sub>N₂</sub> × P<sub>H₂</sub><sup>3</sup>) / P<sub>NH₃</sub><sup>2</sup>

items.q: Calculate Q<sub>p</sub> for the gas in the reactor at that moment.

mistakes.why: Value: you did not cube the pressure of H₂. Its coefficient is 3.
Value: you left out the exponents. Raise each pressure to the power of its coefficient.
Value: you inverted the expression. Products go on top.

items.q: Q<sub>p</sub> for the reactor gas is 8.33 × 10<sup>−6</sup>. What happens to the partial pressure of NH<sub>3</sub> as the gas approaches equilibrium?
options: It increases, because Q<sub>p</sub> < K<sub>p</sub>.
It decreases, because Q<sub>p</sub> < K<sub>p</sub>.
It stays the same, because both values are much less than 1.
It decreases, because there is far more H<sub>2</sub> than NH<sub>3</sub>.

items.q: A student calculates Q<sub>p</sub> using the moles of each gas in the reactor in place of the partial pressures. What is wrong with this approach?
options: K<sub>p</sub> uses partial pressures, so Q<sub>p</sub> has to as well.
Moles are fine, because Q<sub>p</sub> depends on the ratio and not the quantity used.
Moles are fine, as long as the student uses the coefficients as exponents.
Q<sub>p</sub> should use the concentrations in brackets, as K<sub>c</sub> does.

items.q: Which is the equilibrium constant expression for CaCO<sub>3</sub>(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO<sub>2</sub>(g)?
options: K<sub>c</sub> = [CO<sub>2</sub>]
K<sub>c</sub> = [CaO][CO<sub>2</sub>] / [CaCO<sub>3</sub>]
K<sub>c</sub> = [CaO] / [CaCO<sub>3</sub>]
K<sub>c</sub> = 1 / [CO<sub>2</sub>]

items.q: For Zn(s) + Cu<sup>2+</sup>(aq) ⇌ Zn<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + Cu(s), which species appear in the denominator of the expression for K<sub>c</sub>? Select all that apply.
options: Cu<sup>2+</sup>(aq)
Zn<sup>2+</sup>(aq)
Zn(s)
Cu(s)

items.q: Which is the expression for K<sub>c</sub> for CH<sub>3</sub>COOH(aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O(l) ⇌ CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>(aq) + H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>(aq)?
options: [CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>][H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] / [CH<sub>3</sub>COOH]
[CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>][H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] / ([CH<sub>3</sub>COOH][H<sub>2</sub>O])
[CH<sub>3</sub>COOH] / ([CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>][H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>])
[CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>] + [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] − [CH<sub>3</sub>COOH]

items.q: For H<sub>2</sub>(g) + I<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 HI(g), a mixture holds [H<sub>2</sub>] = 0.0150 M, [I<sub>2</sub>] = 0.0300 M and [HI] = 0.0900 M. Calculate Q<sub>c</sub>.

mistakes.why: Value: [HI] must be squared, because its coefficient is 2.
Value: you multiplied [HI] by 2. The coefficient is an exponent: square [HI].
Value: you inverted the expression. Products go on top.

items.q: For a reaction, K = 4.0 × 10<sup>3</sup>. A mixture has Q = 2.5 × 10<sup>4</sup>. Which statement is correct?
options: Q > K, so reactants form until Q falls to K.
Q > K, so products form until Q rises to K.
Q < K, so products form until Q rises to K.
The mixture is at equilibrium, because Q and K are both large.

items.q: Put the steps for predicting which way a mixture will react in order.
options: Write the expression for Q from the balanced equation, leaving out pure solids and liquids.
Substitute the concentrations (or partial pressures) present right now.
Compare the value of Q with the value of K at the same temperature.
Conclude: Q < K net forward; Q > K net reverse; Q = K at equilibrium.

items.q: What is the difference between Q and K for the same reaction at the same temperature?
options: Q uses the amounts present at any moment; K uses the amounts at equilibrium.
Q uses reactants over products; K uses products over reactants.
Q is used for gases; K is used for solutions.
Q includes solids and liquids; K leaves them out.

items.q: For 2 NO(g) + Cl<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 NOCl(g), K<sub>c</sub> = 4.6 × 10<sup>4</sup> at a certain temperature. A mixture at that temperature has [NO] = 0.020 M and [Cl<sub>2</sub>] = 0.010 M. Calculate the [NOCl] for which this mixture would be at equilibrium.

mistakes.why: Value: you found [NOCl]² but did not take the square root. [NOCl] is squared in the expression, so finish with a square root.
Value: [NO] must be squared, because its coefficient is 2.

items.q: Calculate K<sub>c</sub> from the data for trial 1.

mistakes.why: Value: [HI] is squared in K, because its coefficient is 2.
Value: you doubled [HI] instead of squaring it. Coefficients become exponents.
Value: you inverted K. Products go on top.

items.q: Calculate K<sub>c</sub> from the data for trial 3.

mistakes.why: Value: [HI] must be squared, because its coefficient is 2.

items.q: What do the three trials show about K<sub>c</sub>?
options: K<sub>c</sub> is about the same in each trial.
K<sub>c</sub> is largest in the trial with the most HI.
K<sub>c</sub> depends on which substances were put into the flask first.
K<sub>c</sub> is the same because [H<sub>2</sub>] equals [I<sub>2</sub>] in each trial.

items.q: A fourth flask at 450 °C has [H<sub>2</sub>] = 0.0050 M, [I<sub>2</sub>] = 0.0050 M and [HI] = 0.0500 M. Based on the trials, what will happen?
options: HI breaks down, because Q = 100 is greater than K.
More HI forms, because Q = 100 is greater than K.
Nothing, because K changes to match the new mixture.
More HI forms, because [HI] is ten times [H<sub>2</sub>].

items.q: Calculate the initial concentration of NOCl.

mistakes.why: Value: you multiplied moles by volume. Molarity is moles divided by liters.

items.q: Calculate [NOCl] at equilibrium.

mistakes.why: Value: NOCl falls by 2x, not x. Two NOCl react for every Cl₂ that forms.
Value: that is the amount in moles. Divide by the 2.00 L volume to get molarity.

items.q: Use your equilibrium concentrations to calculate K<sub>c</sub> for the decomposition of NOCl at this temperature.

mistakes.why: Value: you used moles instead of concentrations. Divide each amount by 2.00 L first.
Value: [NO] and [NOCl] must be squared, because both have the coefficient 2.
Value: check the changes. NO rises by 2x and NOCl falls by 2x, where x = [Cl₂]; using x for both gives [NO] = 0.0200 M and [NOCl] = 0.230 M.

items.q: Put the steps for finding K<sub>c</sub> in this experiment in order.
options: Convert the moles of NOCl and of Cl<sub>2</sub> to molarities.
Write the ICE table with the change row as −2x, +2x and +x.
Set x equal to the equilibrium [Cl<sub>2</sub>] and fill in the equilibrium row.
Substitute the equilibrium concentrations into the expression for K<sub>c</sub>.

items.q: For N<sub>2</sub>(g) + 3 H<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 NH<sub>3</sub>(g) at a certain temperature, the equilibrium partial pressures are N<sub>2</sub> 0.50 atm, H<sub>2</sub> 1.5 atm and NH<sub>3</sub> 0.12 atm. Calculate K<sub>p</sub>.

mistakes.why: Value: P(H₂) must be cubed, because its coefficient is 3.
Value: raise each pressure to the power of its coefficient.

items.q: Solid NH<sub>4</sub>HS is sealed in an evacuated flask: NH<sub>4</sub>HS(s) ⇌ NH<sub>3</sub>(g) + H<sub>2</sub>S(g). At equilibrium, [NH<sub>3</sub>] = [H<sub>2</sub>S] = 0.0150 M, and 2.00 g of solid remains. Calculate K<sub>c</sub>.

mistakes.why: Value: the solid does not belong in K. Its mass (or amount) never enters the expression.
Value: K is the product of both gas concentrations: [NH₃][H₂S].

items.q: In the NH<sub>4</sub>HS flask, more solid NH<sub>4</sub>HS is added at constant temperature. What happens to [NH<sub>3</sub>]?
options: It stays the same: the solid is not in Q or K.
It increases, because there is more solid to decompose.
It decreases, because the solid absorbs some NH<sub>3</sub>.
It increases until the gas pressure equals the mass of solid.

items.q: Which reaction is a heterogeneous equilibrium?
options: C(s) + H<sub>2</sub>O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + H<sub>2</sub>(g)
N<sub>2</sub>(g) + O<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 NO(g)
2 SO<sub>2</sub>(g) + O<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 SO<sub>3</sub>(g)
Fe<sup>3+</sup>(aq) + SCN<sup>−</sup>(aq) ⇌ FeSCN<sup>2+</sup>(aq)

items.q: A 1.00 L flask starts with 0.200 M CO and 0.200 M H<sub>2</sub>O: CO(g) + H<sub>2</sub>O(g) ⇌ CO<sub>2</sub>(g) + H<sub>2</sub>(g). At equilibrium, [CO<sub>2</sub>] = 0.120 M. Calculate K<sub>c</sub>.

mistakes.why: Value: you used the initial concentrations of CO and H₂O. Use the equilibrium ones: 0.200 − 0.120 = 0.080 M.
Value: K needs every species: [CO₂][H₂] / ([CO][H₂O]).

items.q: A student finds K<sub>c</sub> from the initial concentrations of a reaction mixture instead of the equilibrium ones. Why is the result wrong?
options: K needs equilibrium values; initial ones give Q.
Initial concentrations have too few significant figures.
K needs moles, and concentrations are in molarity.
The initial concentrations should be squared before they are used.

items.q: For A(g) ⇌ 2 B(g), a flask starts with 0.40 M A. At equilibrium [B] = 0.20 M. Which ICE table row is correct for the equilibrium concentrations?
In which reaction does the equilibrium mixture contain almost nothing but reactants?
options: Reaction 1
Reaction 2
Reaction 3
Reaction 4

items.q: The student concludes that reaction 2 must reach equilibrium within seconds because its K is so large. Is the conclusion justified?
options: No: K shows where equilibrium lies, not how fast it is reached.
Yes: a large K means a large rate constant for the forward reaction.
Yes: products form quickly whenever K is greater than 1.
No: a large K means the reaction is slow, because the reverse reaction is fast.

items.q: Which reaction in the table is the most product-favored at equilibrium?
options: Reaction 2
Reaction 3
Reaction 4
Reaction 1

items.q: For reaction 4, a student starts with 1.0 M N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> and predicts that almost all of it will turn into NO<sub>2</sub>. Which response is best?
options: The prediction is wrong: K < 1, so most N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> remains at equilibrium.
The prediction is right: N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> is the one species present at the start.
The prediction is right: K is positive, so products are favored.
The prediction is wrong: no NO<sub>2</sub> forms, because K is less than 1.

items.q: Which reaction has the largest equilibrium constant?
options: Reaction I
Reaction II
Reaction III
They are equal, because each started with the same amounts.

items.q: Each particle in a container stands for 0.10 mol, and each container is 1.0 L. Calculate K<sub>c</sub> for reaction II.

mistakes.why: Value: [XY] is squared, because its coefficient is 2.
Value: you inverted K. Products go on top.

items.q: Which statement about reaction II is correct?
options: Its K is less than 1, so reactants are favored.
Its K is greater than 1, because product is present.
It is not at equilibrium, because it has more reactant than product.
It will react further toward products, because K is small.

items.q: Reaction III is at equilibrium. Which statement compares its forward and reverse rates?
options: They are equal, even though K is not 1.
The forward rate is larger, because K is greater than 1.
The reverse rate is larger, because there are more reactant molecules.
Both rates are zero, because the composition has stopped changing.

items.q: For a reaction at 25 °C, K = 6.0 × 10<sup>−9</sup>. Which describes the equilibrium mixture?
options: Mostly reactants, with a very small amount of products
Mostly products, with a very small amount of reactants
Equal amounts of reactants and products
No products whatsoever

items.q: For a reaction, K = 3 × 10<sup>12</sup>. Which statements are justified? Select all that apply.
options: At equilibrium, products are favored.
Starting from reactants, the reaction goes nearly to completion.
The reaction is fast.
At equilibrium, the forward rate is larger than the reverse rate.

items.q: For A(g) ⇌ 2 B(g), K<sub>c</sub> = 1.0 × 10<sup>−5</sup>. Because K is so small, almost all of the A remains when equilibrium is reached from 0.10 M A. Using [A] ≈ 0.10 M at equilibrium, estimate [B].

mistakes.why: Value: that is [B]². Take the square root to get [B].
Value: set K = [B]² / [A] and solve for [B]; do not divide by the coefficient.

items.q: A cylinder of H<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>2</sub> gases can stand for years without forming water, though K for 2 H<sub>2</sub>(g) + O<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 H<sub>2</sub>O(g) is enormous at room temperature. What explains this?
options: The reaction has a high activation energy, so it is extremely slow at room temperature.
The mixture is already at equilibrium.
K is large, so the reverse reaction prevents water from forming.
K applies once some water has already formed.

items.q: Which value of K describes a reaction in which significant amounts of both reactants and products are present at equilibrium?
For reaction P, K = 1 × 10<sup>4</sup>; for reaction R, K = 1 × 10<sup>−4</sup>. Both start with only reactants. Which statement is correct?
options: P ends with mostly products and R with mostly reactants.
P reaches equilibrium faster than R.
P ends with mostly reactants and R with mostly products.
Both end with equal amounts of reactants and products.

items.q: A student writes: "K for this reaction is 10<sup>−6</sup>, so no reaction occurs and there is nothing to study." Which response is best?
options: Disagree: a little product forms before equilibrium.
Agree: a K below 10<sup>−3</sup> means the reaction does not happen.
Disagree: a small K means the reaction is fast, so it reaches equilibrium at once.
Agree: K is so small that the reverse reaction stops the forward one.

items.q: For the same reaction, which statement about K and Q is correct?
options: K is fixed at a given temperature; Q changes as the mixture changes.
Q is fixed at a given temperature; K changes as the mixture changes.
Both change as the mixture changes.
Neither changes once the reactants are mixed.

items.q: Calculate K<sub>c</sub> for 2 NO<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 NO(g) + O<sub>2</sub>(g).

mistakes.why: Value: reversing a reaction does not change the sign of K. Take the reciprocal: 1/K.
Value: you took a square root. The coefficients are unchanged; only the direction is reversed, so use 1/K.

items.q: Calculate K<sub>c</sub> for NO(g) + ½ O<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ NO<sub>2</sub>(g).

mistakes.why: Value: halving the coefficients does not halve K. It raises K to the power ½: take the square root.
Value: you squared K. Halving the coefficients takes the square root.

items.q: Reactions A and B can be combined to describe nitrogen dioxide forming directly from the elements. Use the table to calculate K<sub>c</sub> at 25 °C for N<sub>2</sub>(g) + 2 O<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 NO<sub>2</sub>(g).

mistakes.why: Value: you added the K values. When reactions are added, their K values are multiplied.
Value: you divided. Adding reaction A to reaction B means multiplying K<sub>A</sub> by K<sub>B</sub>.

items.q: Which operation gives K<sub>c</sub> for 4 NO(g) ⇌ 2 N<sub>2</sub>(g) + 2 O<sub>2</sub>(g)?
options: (1/K<sub>A</sub>)<sup>2</sup>
2/(K<sub>A</sub>)
(K<sub>A</sub>)<sup>2</sup>
−2K<sub>A</sub>

items.q: Using the values in the table, is N<sub>2</sub>(g) + 2 O<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 NO<sub>2</sub>(g) product-favored at this temperature?
options: No: K = 2.7 × 10<sup>−17</sup>, far below 1.
Yes: reaction B has a large K, so the overall reaction does too.
Yes: K = 6.0 × 10<sup>13</sup> + 4.5 × 10<sup>−31</sup>, which is large.
It is undecided, because K<sub>A</sub> and K<sub>B</sub> point in opposite directions.

items.q: A flask at 350 K holds an equilibrium mixture. More N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> is injected and the flask is held at 350 K. What is K<sub>c</sub> once equilibrium is restored?
options: Greater than 0.13, because more N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> reacts.
Less than 0.13, because there is more reactant on the bottom of the expression.
1.5, because the system shifts to the next K in the table.

items.q: What does the table show about this reaction as the temperature rises?
options: It becomes more product-favored.
It becomes more reactant-favored.
It reaches equilibrium more slowly.
Its K stays the same, but its Q increases.

items.q: Calculate K<sub>c</sub> for 2 NO<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>(g) at 400 K.

mistakes.why: Value: this is K for the forward direction. Reversing a reaction gives 1/K.
Value: reversing does not make K negative. Take the reciprocal.

items.q: A student says K<sub>c</sub> increased from 298 K to 450 K because more N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> was added in the hotter trials. Which response is best?
options: Wrong: K changed because the temperature changed.
Right: K grows when there is more reactant to react.
Right: at higher temperatures there are more molecules, so K rises.
Wrong: K is a fixed number, so the table contains an error.

items.q: For 2 SO<sub>2</sub>(g) + O<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 SO<sub>3</sub>(g), K<sub>c</sub> = K. What is K<sub>c</sub> for SO<sub>2</sub>(g) + ½ O<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ SO<sub>3</sub>(g)?
options: K<sup>1/2</sup>
2K

items.q: For H<sub>2</sub>(g) + I<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 HI(g), K<sub>c</sub> = 50.0 at 450 °C. Calculate K<sub>c</sub> for HI(g) ⇌ ½ H<sub>2</sub>(g) + ½ I<sub>2</sub>(g) at 450 °C.

mistakes.why: Value: reversing gives 1/50.0, but you also halved the equation. Take the square root as well.
Value: halving an equation takes a square root; it does not divide K by 2.
Value: you halved the equation but did not reverse it. Take the reciprocal too.

items.q: Given: (1) A(g) ⇌ B(g), K<sub>1</sub> = 1.4 × 10<sup>−2</sup>; (2) B(g) ⇌ 2 C(g), K<sub>2</sub> = 6.0 × 10<sup>−5</sup>. Calculate K for A(g) ⇌ 2 C(g).

mistakes.why: Value: when reactions add, their K values multiply.
Value: neither reaction is reversed, so multiply the K values rather than dividing.

items.q: Given: CO(g) + H<sub>2</sub>O(g) ⇌ CO<sub>2</sub>(g) + H<sub>2</sub>(g), K<sub>1</sub>; and CH<sub>4</sub>(g) + H<sub>2</sub>O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + 3 H<sub>2</sub>(g), K<sub>2</sub>. Which gives K for CH<sub>4</sub>(g) + 2 H<sub>2</sub>O(g) ⇌ CO<sub>2</sub>(g) + 4 H<sub>2</sub>(g)?
options: K<sub>1</sub>K<sub>2</sub>
K<sub>1</sub> + K<sub>2</sub>
K<sub>2</sub> / K<sub>1</sub>
(K<sub>1</sub> × K<sub>2</sub>)<sup>2</sup>

items.q: Hess’s law (topic 6.9) says ΔH values add when equations add. Why are K values multiplied instead?
options: K is a product of terms, so shared terms cancel.
K values are larger in size than ΔH values are.
K depends on temperature and ΔH does not.
Multiplying is used so the units of K cancel.

items.q: For N<sub>2</sub>(g) + 3 H<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 NH<sub>3</sub>(g), K<sub>c</sub> = 0.50 at a certain temperature. Calculate K<sub>c</sub> for 2 N<sub>2</sub>(g) + 6 H<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 4 NH<sub>3</sub>(g).

mistakes.why: Value: doubling the equation squares K; it does not double it.

items.q: Which changes alter the value of K<sub>c</sub> for a given reaction equation? Select all that apply.
options: Changing the temperature
Adding more of a reactant
Changing the volume of the container
Adding a catalyst
